title: Implicit biases are harder to change in big cities than in small cities
gist: A Santa Fe Institute study published in PNAS finds a narrative intervention reduces implicit bias in every US city, but the effect persists nine days in cities of around 150,000 residents while decaying within twenty-four hours in cities of millions — because dense urban information flows dilute any single new experience. The practical implication is that corporate bias-training effectiveness is a function of city size and timing relative to the decision it is meant to influence.

themes.theme: City scale as a moderator of attitude change

insights.claim: A single narrative intervention reduced implicit bias in participants across every US city regardless of population size, but the durability of the effect scaled inversely with city size: nine days in cities of roughly 150,000 residents versus under twenty-four hours in cities of millions.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Any behaviour-change programme measured only on immediate post-test effects will systematically overstate durability in dense markets.
insights.locator: While the story reduced participants’ biases

insights.claim: Implicit biases are malleable reflections of everyday experience rather than fixed traits, meaning population-level bias measures should move with the local information environment rather than being treated as stable demographic constants.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Treat measured social attitudes as a dynamic, environment-driven variable when modelling consumer or workforce sentiment across geographies.

insights.claim: The researcher characterises the result as the first strong proof that biases are contextual rather than individually fixed.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: A claimed first-of-kind result raises the odds of follow-on replication studies and of policy bodies revising intervention guidance.
insights.quote: the first strong proof of how contextual biases are

insights.claim: Big-city residents already interact with outgroup members frequently, so one additional positive experience is a marginal addition to a large base and moves the needle little — whereas in small cities the intervention may be a participant's first such experience and therefore shifts opinion sharply.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Marginal-experience-per-baseline is a transferable model for why messaging saturates faster in dense markets than sparse ones.
insights.locator: Stier attributes this difference to two qualities

insights.claim: Big cities deliver a constant stream of competing signals — interpersonal interactions, advertisements, TVs in restaurants, ambient music and phone content — that dilutes any single intervention, so quieter small cities let one message persist far longer.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Directly implies higher required message frequency and spend to hold share of mind in large metros — a structural cost asymmetry for urban-focused campaigns.
insights.quote: let alone what we see on our phones,
insights.locator: Second, big-city dwellers have a constant stream

insights.claim: Shifting the attitudes of large-city populations requires a heftier intervention than in small cities to overcome the ambient information load, making cost-per-attitude-change a rising function of urban scale.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Budget models that assume flat cost-per-impression across geographies understate the true cost of persuasion in megacities.
insights.locator: So it makes sense that it will take a heftier intervention

insights.claim: Companies using implicit bias interventions to reduce biased hiring decisions should factor in the population size of the city they operate in, because identical training yields materially different persistence by location.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Multi-site employers running one uniform DEI training programme are likely getting uneven and partly wasted effect — a measurable HR-spend efficiency gap.

insights.claim: Big-city employers should schedule bias interventions immediately before the hiring decision they are meant to influence, since the effect wanes within a day — a reframing of intervention design from content to timing.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Timing-based delivery favours just-in-time, workflow-embedded training tools over annual classroom sessions — a product-design signal for HR software.
insights.quote: That’s a pretty big reframing of how we think about the design of these interventions

insights.claim: The evidence combines an online implicit-association test taken by millions of participants across US cities with a controlled arm of 1,150 participants who took the test, read a story in which an outgroup member helped them through a stressful situation such as terminal illness or homelessness, then retook the test repeatedly over the following days.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Large observational sample plus a repeated-measures experimental arm makes this harder to dismiss than typical single-shot bias-training studies.
insights.locator: Stier analyzed the results of an online test

insights.claim: The findings are published in PNAS on 6 August 2026 as "Implicit biases change more slowly in larger cities" (DOI 10.1073/pnas.2514189123), authored by a Complexity Postdoctoral Fellow at the Santa Fe Institute.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Peer-reviewed placement in a top general-science journal raises the chance of downstream policy and corporate adoption of the timing insight.
